outcome_intro: Cisco Meraki plus your AI answers the questions that span every client org at once: what is down right now and since when, which licenses and hardware hit their end date this quarter, who changed what across all orgs this week, and which change landed just before a site dropped. One API key, every org it can reach, every page of every org read by the fleet views, and an org that fails to answer is named instead of silently counted as zero.

instead_of_say.instead: Opening the MSP Portal, spotting an org with a red device count, then clicking into that org and its networks to find which device is offline and how long it has been down - once per client
instead_of_say.say: What is down across all my Meraki clients right now?

instead_of_say.instead: Checking each org's license page by hand, because the portal shows only one co-term date per org and nothing for per-device, subscription, or end-of-support hardware, before the renewal quotes are due
instead_of_say.say: Which Meraki licenses, subscriptions, and end-of-support dates hit in the next 90 days?

instead_of_say.instead: Scrolling one org's change log against the outage time after a site goes down, trying to work out whether a tech's change caused it
instead_of_say.say: Did someone change something right before this switch went offline?

pain_points: Meraki's MSP Portal lists each organization with device counts, license status, and one co-terminated license expiration date (Meraki documentation, 'Monitoring and Managing Multiple Organizations'). What it documents is per-org counts: no cross-org list of which devices are down, no cross-org change log, no admin management across orgs. Answering 'what is down for every client' still means clicking into each org.

Meraki's paginated list endpoints return a bare JSON array and page only through an RFC 5988 Link header (ten items per page by default on many of them), so a script that reads one response silently stops at page one. The Meraki Community Developers & APIs board has threads such as 'Using Powershell how to paginate thru pages' and 'Meraki API - Get Organization Clients Search - Only return 3 networks' working through exactly that.

Renewals follow three licensing models - co-termination, per-device, and subscription - plus end-of-sale and end-of-support dates on hardware, so one date-sorted list of what is due across all clients does not exist in the Dashboard.

different_vs_wrappers: Most Meraki integrations, including the many single-org Meraki MCP servers, proxy one question into one live API call against one organization, and often read only the first page of a list. This connector is built for the MSP case: the fleet commands run across every org the key can see under one rate limiter, follow every Link-header page, and keep an org that fails to answer in the result as unreachable instead of reporting zero devices. It also wraps all 1,035 Dashboard operations as typed commands, and a single-endpoint read through MCP says when Meraki has more pages instead of passing page one off as the whole list.
different_vs_vendor: The Meraki Dashboard and its MSP Portal stay the place you configure networks; the portal, as Meraki documents it, shows per-org device counts and one co-term date. This adds the cross-org answers on top: a single list of what is down with network names and downtime, renewals across all three licensing models plus end-of-support hardware, one change log for every org, admin two-factor and offboarding checks, and the config changes made just before an outage.

faqs.a: Yes, on paid ChatGPT plans. ChatGPT connects to remote MCP servers over HTTPS, and cisco-meraki-mcp speaks HTTP natively: set CISCO_MERAKI_MCP_HTTP_TOKEN, run `cisco-meraki-mcp --transport http`, and put its /mcp endpoint behind an HTTPS tunnel or your own reverse proxy. Step-by-step in the install guide.

faqs.q: Do I need to know how to code?
faqs.a: No. Paste one sentence into Claude Code or Codex and your agent does the install, or run a one-line installer. You enter your Meraki API key once.

faqs.q: Is my Cisco Meraki data safe?
faqs.a: Your data stays on your machine. The CLI, MCP server, and the optional local mirror all run locally and talk only to the Meraki Dashboard API. The AI sees query results, not raw bulk data, and your API key is never bundled or transmitted by MSP Skills.
Free. Apache-2.0 licensed. You pay only for whichever AI agent you already use.

faqs.q: What can the API key reach?
faqs.a: A Meraki API key carries the Dashboard permissions of the admin account that generated it, across every organization that admin can see. Generate it from an admin with read-only access if you only want reporting. Each org must also have Dashboard API access enabled (Organization > Settings); an org without it shows up in `fleet health` as reachable: false rather than disappearing.

faqs.q: Will this hit my Meraki API rate limit?
faqs.a: Meraki allows about ten calls per second per organization. The CLI paces itself at 10 requests per second by default (change it with --rate-limit) and, when Meraki answers HTTP 429, waits for the Retry-After header before trying again. Fleet commands across many orgs take longer: each run has one overall --timeout (default 1m), so raise it (for example --timeout 10m) for a large fleet; an org that runs out of time is reported as partial, not silently dropped.

faqs.q: Does it work with the Canada, China, India, or FedRAMP dashboards?
faqs.a: Yes. Set CISCO_MERAKI_BASE_URL to your region's API host, for example https://api.meraki.ca/api/v1 (Canada), https://api.meraki.cn/api/v1 (China), https://api.meraki.in/api/v1 (India), or https://api.gov-meraki.com/api/v1 (FedRAMP). Leave it unset for the global dashboard.

faqs.q: Can an agent change my clients' networks by accident?
faqs.a: Writes send immediately when called, with no confirmation prompt, so keep autonomous agents to reads and --dry-run previews. The bulk tool, fleet push, previews a per-network diff by default and sends nothing unless you add --apply. See the safety model for which commands to keep behind a human. Set CISCO_MERAKI_MCP_READ_ONLY=1 on the MCP server and it refuses every write outright.

governance_summary: Reads - the fleet views, every GET, sync and search - change nothing in the Dashboard and are safe for an agent, with one exception: about twenty reads return live secrets or license keys (SSID pre-shared keys, identity PSK passphrases, SNMP community strings, site-to-site VPN peer secrets, BGP and OSPF passwords, Apple VPP tokens, license keys, and the raw configuration change log, which records API request bodies) and the CLI does not redact them, so those belong behind a human. Routine config writes should be previewed with --dry-run and approved. Bulk pushes, reboots and port cycles, admin and SAML changes, API key generation, and deletes or unclaims should never run unattended. For an MCP agent that should never write, CISCO_MERAKI_MCP_READ_ONLY=1 makes the server refuse every non-GET call. The real ceiling is the API key: it can do whatever the Dashboard admin who generated it can do.

safety_tiers.policy: Human-in-the-loop only - never in a blanket allow-all-reads policy, and do not hand the raw output to a model
